influences/fish-chi-rho-symbols/name: Early symbols: fish, anchor, Chi-Rho and the cross
influences/fish-chi-rho-symbols/sourceCu: Common Graeco-Roman motifs (fish, anchor, dove, ship), the Greek chi-rho ligature used as an abbreviation, and the Roman cross as an instrument of execution
influences/fish-chi-rho-symbols/christia: The ichthys acrostic, the anchor of hope, the Chi-Rho monogram, the staurogram and the cross as Christian emblems
influences/fish-chi-rho-symbols/evidence: The popular claims that the fish is a pagan fertility symbol, that the cross is the Tammuz ‘tau’ and that the Chi-Rho was a solar emblem lack evidence. What is true is that Christians used ordinary graphic forms: anchors, fish and doves were everyday motifs, and the chi-rho ligature existed as an abbreviation before Christ. Christian meanings for these symbols are explicitly documented in second- and third-century texts.
influences/fish-chi-rho-symbols/popularC: Christian symbols are pagan in origin: the fish (ichthys) comes from the fertility cults of Atargatis or Dagon, the cross from the ‘T’ of Tammuz, and Constantine’s Chi-Rho was really a sun symbol.
influences/fish-chi-rho-symbols/whatHist: Christian authors of c. 180–230 explain the meaning of their symbols in their own words. Tertullian (De baptismo 1) and the Abercius inscription use the fish for Christ; the acrostic ΙΧΘΥΣ (‘Jesus Christ, Son of God, Saviour’) appears in the Sibylline Oracles (8.217–250) quoted by Augustine; Clement of Alexandria lists the dove, fish, ship and anchor as suitable seal-ring images (Paedagogus 3.11). The anchor draws on Hebrews 6:19. The cross was the instrument of Jesus’s execution, as the Gospels and the anti-Christian Alexamenos graffito (c. 200) show, and the ‘staurogram’ appears in Gospel papyri (P66, P75) before Constantine. The chi-rho ligature had been used on Ptolemaic coins and as a scribal mark, and Constantine adopted it as Christ’s monogram in 312 according to Lactantius. Historians see the reuse of everyday graphic forms, not the adoption of pagan religious symbols.
influences/fish-chi-rho-symbols/summary: The first Christian symbols, the fish, anchor, dove, Chi-Rho and cross, used ordinary forms of the Roman world but had explicitly Christian meanings attested in early texts; claims of pagan religious origin do not stand up to the evidence.
influences/fish-chi-rho-symbols/story:
Before Christians made pictures of Christ they used signs. Clement of Alexandria, writing c. 200, told believers that their seal rings should not bear idols, swords or wine-cups but a dove, a fish, a ship running before the wind, a lyre or an anchor, and that a fisherman would remind them of the apostles and the children drawn from the water (Paedagogus 3.11). The list shows both continuity and choice: these were stock motifs of Roman gem-cutters, selected because they could carry Christian meaning.

The fish is the best documented. The Greek word ΙΧΘΥΣ forms an acrostic of Iēsous Christos Theou Huios Sōtēr, ‘Jesus Christ, Son of God, Saviour’, worked into an acrostic poem in the Sibylline Oracles (8.217–250) which Augustine later quoted (City of God 18.23). Tertullian wrote c. 200 that ‘we little fishes, after the example of our Ichthys Jesus Christ, are born in water’ (De baptismo 1). The epitaph of Abercius of Hierapolis in Phrygia (before 216) speaks of eating ‘the fish from the spring, very great and pure’, and the Pectorius inscription at Autun uses the same imagery. Gospel stories of fishermen, the feeding of the multitudes and the risen Christ’s meal of fish reinforced the symbol. The Syrian goddess Atargatis did have sacred fish, as Lucian notes, but there is no evidence that Christians drew on her cult.

The anchor, common on pagan tombstones as a sailor’s emblem, became for Christians the ‘anchor of the soul’ (Hebrews 6:19), often shaped so that its stock suggested a cross; it is frequent in the Catacomb of Priscilla and on early epitaphs. The dove carried the olive branch of Noah and the Spirit of Jesus’s baptism. The cross itself was rarely depicted before the fourth century: Roman crucifixion was a shameful death, and a graffito on the Palatine (c. 200) mocks a Christian named Alexamenos for worshipping a crucified figure with a donkey’s head. Yet Christians traced the sign of the cross on their foreheads (Tertullian, De corona 3); Justin Martyr saw the cross shape everywhere in nature, in masts, ploughs and the human form (1 Apology 55); and Minucius Felix insisted that Christians did not worship crosses (Octavius 29). Larry Hurtado and Bruce Longenecker have shown that the staurogram, a tau-rho ligature depicting the crucified Jesus, was used in Christian manuscripts c. 200 and that cross imagery existed before Constantine.

The Chi-Rho monogram, formed from the first two Greek letters of Christos, came to prominence with Constantine. Lactantius, a contemporary, reports that before the battle of the Milvian Bridge (312) Constantine was told in a dream to mark ‘the heavenly sign of God’ on his soldiers’ shields, a letter X with its top bent round, i.e. the Chi-Rho (De mortibus persecutorum 44). Eusebius’s later account describes a vision of a cross of light with the words ‘By this conquer’ and the jewelled standard, the labarum (Life of Constantine 1.28–31). The ligature itself was not new: it appears on coins of Ptolemy III and as a scribe’s abbreviation for chrēston (‘useful’). Constantine’s silver medallion from Ticinum (c. 315) shows the Chi-Rho on his helmet, and the monogram was soon ubiquitous on sarcophagi, lamps and church furnishings.

In the modern era some groups have rejected the cross as pagan. Alexander Hislop’s The Two Babylons (1853) traced it to the Tammuz ‘tau’, and from the 1930s Jehovah’s Witnesses abandoned the cross, teaching that Jesus died on an upright stake (‘torture stake’ in the New World Translation). Historians note that Greek stauros and Latin crux were used of crosses of several shapes, that Roman sources describe crucifixion with a crossbeam (patibulum), and that early Christian writers already took the cross shape for granted. The borrowing in this story is of forms: an alphabet, a vocabulary of motifs and a Roman instrument of death, given new meaning by a community that proclaimed a crucified Messiah.
influences/fish-chi-rho-symbols/howItHap: Christians chose from the existing repertoire of Roman gem, lamp and tomb motifs those that could bear Christian meaning.
Wordplay and acrostics, such as ΙΧΘΥΣ, gave ordinary images a confessional content intelligible to insiders.
Biblical texts (Hebrews 6:19, Genesis 8, the Gospel fish stories) supplied the meanings of the anchor, dove and fish.
Scribes developed the nomina sacra and the staurogram, turning letter combinations into visual references to Christ and his cross.
Constantine’s adoption of the Chi-Rho in 312 made Christian symbols public, imperial and military.
influences/fish-chi-rho-symbols/examples: Fish and bread-basket paintings in the Crypts of Lucina, Catacomb of Callixtus, Rome (early third century).
Epitaph of Abercius of Hierapolis (late second century), fragments in the Vatican Museums.
Anchors and fish on third-century epitaphs in the Catacomb of Priscilla, Rome.
Staurogram in the Bodmer papyri P66 and P75 (c. 175–225).
Chi-Rho on Constantine’s helmet on the Ticinum silver medallion (c. 315), and on fourth-century ‘passion’ sarcophagi.
influences/fish-chi-rho-symbols/defender: Recommended the dove, fish, ship, lyre and anchor as seal-ring images, reinterpreting common motifs for Christian use (Paedagogus 3.11).
Explained the fish as a baptismal symbol (De baptismo 1) and described Christians signing their foreheads with the cross (De corona 3).
Argued that the shape of the cross was imprinted throughout nature and human culture, from ships’ masts to military standards (1 Apology 55).
Recorded Constantine’s vision and described the labarum with its Chi-Rho (Life of Constantine 1.28–31).
influences/fish-chi-rho-symbols/critics/: Claimed in The Two Babylons (1853) that the cross derived from the mystic ‘tau’ of Tammuz, an assertion without ancient evidence.
Since the 1930s have rejected the cross as a pagan symbol, teaching that Jesus died on a single upright stake.
influences/fish-chi-rho-symbols/keptBy/0: Virtually all Christian traditions use the cross; Catholic, Orthodox, Oriental and Anglican churches also use the crucifix.
influences/fish-chi-rho-symbols/keptBy/1: Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches use the Chi-Rho on vestments, altars and Easter candles.
influences/fish-chi-rho-symbols/keptBy/2: Many modern Protestants use the ichthys as a badge of faith.
influences/fish-chi-rho-symbols/rejected: Jehovah’s Witnesses, who reject the cross.
Some Reformed and Puritan Christians, who removed crucifixes and cross ornaments from churches as idolatrous, while keeping the doctrine of the cross.
influences/sunday-day-of-the-sun/name: Sunday, the "day of the sun" and Constantine's law of 321
influences/sunday-day-of-the-sun/sourceC: The planetary 'day of the Sun' (dies Solis) and Roman civic rest days
influences/sunday-day-of-the-sun/christi: The Lord's Day (kyriake, dies dominica) as the weekly day of worship and, from 321, of legal rest
influences/sunday-day-of-the-sun/evidenc: The claim that Constantine moved Christian worship from Saturday to Sunday is false. Sunday worship is attested about two centuries before him, in Revelation 1:10, the Didache 14, Ignatius (Magnesians 9) and Justin Martyr (First Apology 67, c.155). Some things really are Roman. The name 'Sunday' in Germanic languages is pagan, and so is Constantine's decision to make the 'venerable day of the Sun' a civic rest day (Codex Justinianus 3.12.2, 7 March 321). Samuele Bacchiocchi argued that sun-cult influence shaped the second-century choice of Sunday. This is a minority view among scholars.
influences/sunday-day-of-the-sun/popular: Christians originally kept the seventh-day Sabbath until Constantine, a sun-worshipper, changed it to Sunday by imperial decree in 321, so Sunday worship is a pagan sun cult.
influences/sunday-day-of-the-sun/whatHis: The New Testament already associates the first day of the week with the resurrection, gatherings and collections (Mark 16:2, Acts 20:7, 1 Corinthians 16:2), and Revelation 1:10 speaks of 'the Lord's day'. Second-century sources describe Sunday assemblies as normal. Justin explained to a pagan emperor that Christians met 'on the day called of the Sun' because it was the first day of creation and the day of Christ's resurrection. Constantine's law of 321 did not create Christian Sunday worship. It gave an existing Christian custom civic force, using neutral solar language acceptable to pagan subjects. The day became a day of rest only gradually. For centuries it was mainly a day of worship, and conciliar rulings such as Laodicea canon 29 encouraged Christians to work on Saturday and rest, if possible, on Sunday. D. A. Carson's symposium From Sabbath to Lord's Day (1982) answered Bacchiocchi and represents the mainstream view.
influences/sunday-day-of-the-sun/summary: Christians met for worship on the first day of the week, the day of the resurrection, long before Constantine. What came from Rome was the planetary name 'day of the Sun', kept in English and German, and Constantine's 321 law making that day a legal rest day.
influences/sunday-day-of-the-sun/story:
The Jewish seven-day week, ending with the Sabbath, was the framework within which the first Christians lived. The Gospels place the resurrection 'on the first day of the week', and Paul's churches gathered and set aside money on that day (1 Corinthians 16:2). By the end of the first century the author of Revelation could call it 'the Lord's day' (kyriake hemera). The Didache tells believers to gather 'on the Lord's own day' to break bread. Ignatius of Antioch (c.110) described Jewish converts as 'no longer sabbatising but living according to the Lord's day, on which our life also arose' (Magnesians 9). The Epistle of Barnabas called it the joyful 'eighth day'.

Meanwhile the Greco-Roman world was adopting a different seven-day cycle, the planetary week. Each day was named after one of the seven 'planets' in astrological order: Saturn, Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus. Graffiti at Pompeii list the days, and Cassius Dio, writing c.230, said the custom had recently become universal. In this cycle the Christian first day fell on the 'day of the Sun'. Justin Martyr, writing his First Apology in Rome c.155, used that civil name for his pagan readers: 'on the day called of the Sun all who live in cities or in the country gather in one place'.

Constantine's law of 7 March 321 ordered magistrates, city dwellers and workshops to rest 'on the venerable day of the Sun' (venerabili die Solis). Farmers were exempted so that harvests would not be lost. A second law of July 321 permitted the emancipation and manumission of slaves on that day (Codex Theodosianus 2.8.1). Eusebius' Life of Constantine (4.18–20) presents the measure as honouring the Lord's Day. The emperor also gave pagan soldiers a monotheistic prayer to say on Sundays. The deliberately neutral wording suited an emperor whose coins still showed Sol Invictus, but the custom it protected was already Christian.

The names show where the influence lay. Greek-speaking and Romance-speaking Christians renamed the day after the Lord: kyriake, domenica, domingo, dimanche. Russian calls it voskresenie, 'resurrection'. English, German and Dutch kept the pagan Sunday, and Christian writers from Justin onwards made a virtue of it, calling Christ the 'sun of righteousness' (Malachi 4:2) who rose at dawn. Jerome wrote that if pagans call it the day of the sun, Christians gladly agree, for on it the Light of the world arose.

The Constantine story became central in nineteenth-century Sabbatarian controversy. Seventh Day Baptists (from the 1650s) and then Seventh-day Adventists, notably Ellen G. White, taught that the change from Sabbath to Sunday was a human and papal innovation. Samuele Bacchiocchi's From Sabbath to Sunday (1977) gave the case its most scholarly form, locating the change in Hadrianic Rome. Most historians accept that Sunday worship is pre-Constantinian and grounded in the resurrection. They also accept that the legal Sunday and the English name are Roman inheritances.
influences/sunday-day-of-the-sun/howItHa: Apostolic communities gathered on the first day of the week in memory of the resurrection (Acts 20:7; 1 Corinthians 16:2; Revelation 1:10).
Second-century writers (Didache, Ignatius, Barnabas, Justin) treat the Lord's Day assembly as standard.
The planetary week spread across the Roman empire in the first and second centuries, putting the Christian first day on the 'day of the Sun'.
Constantine made the dies Solis a civic rest day in 321, protecting Christian worship in neutral language.
Later councils and emperors (Laodicea, Theodosius I, Justinian) extended Sunday restrictions on work and entertainments.
influences/sunday-day-of-the-sun/example: Justin Martyr, First Apology 67: 'on the day called of the Sun' Christians read the apostles and prophets and celebrate the Eucharist.
Codex Justinianus 3.12.2 (321): 'Let all judges, city people and craftsmen rest on the venerable day of the Sun.'
Pliny the Younger (Letters 10.96, c.112) reports Christians meeting 'on a fixed day before dawn'.
Romance-language names (domingo, dimanche, domenica) versus the Germanic 'Sunday' and 'Sonntag'.
influences/sunday-day-of-the-sun/defende: Used the civil name 'day of the Sun' to explain Christian worship to pagans, grounding it in creation and resurrection.
Praised Constantine's Sunday legislation as honouring the 'Lord's and Saviour's day' (Life of Constantine 4.18).
Contrasted sabbatising with 'living according to the Lord's day', the earliest post-biblical theology of Sunday.
influences/sunday-day-of-the-sun/critics: Ellen G. White and the Seventh-day Adventists
Taught that Sunday observance was a human and papal substitution for the biblical Sabbath, to be tested in the last days.
Argued in From Sabbath to Sunday (1977) that anti-Judaism and sun-cult symbolism in second-century Rome produced the shift to Sunday. This is a minority scholarly view.
From the 1650s in England, kept Saturday as the only biblical Sabbath.
influences/sunday-day-of-the-sun/keptBy/: Almost all Catholic, Orthodox, Oriental and Protestant churches (Sunday as the Lord's Day)
Reformed and Puritan Sabbatarians, who transferred Sabbath rules to Sunday (Westminster Confession 21)
influences/sunday-day-of-the-sun/rejecte: Church of God (Seventh Day) and some Messianic Jewish congregations
